steps.html:
An egg bought for scrap turns out to be worth thirty-two million dollars. A couple find eight tins of gold coins on their own land. Four true stories, and the question underneath all of them: what must you hand in, and what can you keep?

  • Listen to four news items for gist and detail
  • Use must, have to, should, can't and needn't accurately
  • Write about what the law should require you to do

steps.title: Obligation, prohibition, advice, and the absence of obligation
steps.html:
The complete rule first, then a large example bank, then practice.

Must and have to both express obligation, but they come from different places. Must is the speaker's own sense of what is necessary: I must hand this in. Have to is an outside rule: You have to hand it in — it's the law.

The strongest trap is the negative. Mustn't = it is forbidden. Don't have to and needn't = there is no obligation either way. You mustn't keep it and You don't have to keep it mean opposite things.

Can gives permission, can't refuses it or states impossibility. Should and ought to give advice, not orders.

Modals have no -s, no do, and are followed by the bare infinitive: She must hand it in. — never She musts or She must to hand.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences built on the four news stories.

You must report a find of this size.
The speaker's own judgement of what is necessary.

In Italy you have to hand lost property to the police.
An external legal rule.

He had to wait a year before he could sell it.
Have to has a past form; must does not.

You mustn't keep something you know is stolen.
Prohibition — this is forbidden.

You don't have to accept the reward.
No obligation. Completely different from mustn't.

You needn't bring the receipt.
Same meaning as don't have to, slightly more formal.

The couple can take ownership if no owner is found.
Permission.

You can't claim it while the owner is still traceable.
Prohibition or impossibility.

He should have the paintings valued.
Advice, not an order.

They ought to return the bag to the dealer.
Ought to keeps the to.

Anybody may inspect the register.
Formal permission.

She must be the owner — her name is inside the bag.
Must can also express a confident deduction.

steps.title: Choosing between mustn't and don't have to
steps.html:
1. The situation: the law says a finder is free to keep an item after a year, but selling it before then is forbidden.
  2. 'Selling it before then is forbidden' is a prohibition, so: You mustn't sell it during the first year.
  3. 'A finder is free to keep it' means there is no obligation to give it up, so: You don't have to give it back after a year.
  4. Test yourself by asking: is the action banned, or simply not required? Banned → mustn't. Not required → don't have to / needn't.
  5. Never mix them: You mustn't give it back would mean returning it is illegal, which is not what the law says.

steps.title: Write your opinion.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Say what the law requires now, what it should require, and why.
steps.html:
• State what the law requires now, using <i>have to</i>.
  • Say what you think it should require, using <i>should</i> or <i>ought to</i>.
  • Name one thing that must never be allowed, using <i>mustn't</i>.
  • Name one thing that should not be required, using <i>don't have to</i> or <i>needn't</i>.

Useful language

  • Under the current law you have to …
  • In practice, most people don't have to …
  • In my view, finders should / ought to …
  • What you certainly mustn't do is …
  • There is no reason why anyone should have to …
  • The rule can't be fair if …
steps.modelHtml:
Money found in the street

Under the current law here, you have to hand in anything you find that is worth more than a small amount, and the police keep it for a year. If nobody claims it, you can take ownership. In practice almost nobody reports a £20 note, and I do not think they should have to.

The rule works badly at the edges. A wallet with a name inside is different: you mustn't keep that, because the owner is traceable in thirty seconds. A note lying on an empty pavement is not traceable at all, and forcing people to report it only teaches them to ignore the law.

My view is that the test ought to be traceability, not value. If the owner can be found, you must try. If not, the finder needn't do anything at all.
